clue.text: Harbour overseer expecting masses of people to arrive

definitions.text: Harbour overseer expecting masses of people to arrive

parts.words: Harbour overseer expecting masses of people to arrive
parts.note: a cryptic description of the monument standing over New York harbour, whose plaque welcomes the 'huddled masses' arriving by ship

explanation.surface: A harbourmaster braces for crowds of passengers coming ashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbour overseer' sounds like a port official, but it is a statue that literally looks over the harbour; Emma Lazarus's poem on its base invites the 'huddled masses' of immigrants.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York monument greets incoming immigrants and stands watch over the harbour, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Swain embraces love a lot

indicators.note: embraces means the word for the swain holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: a swain is a young lover or country lad
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A young suitor hugs his sweetheart and loves her greatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A load, as in 'a load of money', is informal for a great quantity.

clue.text: Attachment to ship violating a night at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the preceding letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Something fixed to a vessel breaks the rules of a dark night voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' fits the nautical surface but signals the rearrangement of VIOLATING A NIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel carries coloured lamps fixed to its hull and mast so others can see its position and heading after dark.

clue.text: Take to water, about to abandon attempt to take in air

indicators.note: to abandon tells us the letters for 'about' leave the longer word

parts.note: to draw breath is to try to take air into the lungs
re is Latin-derived for 'concerning', i.e. about

explanation.surface: A swimmer gives up gasping for breath and plunges into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to abandon' removes RE (about) from BREATHE.
explanation.definitionFit: To go swimming or wash in a lake or sea is to take to the water.

clue.text: A lot of legal information about British criminal activity

indicators.note: about means the shortened word goes around the next piece
a lot of means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a brief is the set of instructions and facts given to a barrister

explanation.surface: A barrister's file holds plenty of facts concerning a British crime spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' trims BRIEF to BRIE, which goes 'about' B.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying an official to act improperly is a criminal offence, an example of illegal activity.

clue.text: The dancer, losing head, botched this at first!

definitions.text: The dancer, losing head, botched this at first!

indicators.note: botched means messed up, so the gathered letters are rearranged
losing head means the first letter of dancer is removed
at first takes only the opening letter of this

explanation.surface: A performer, distracted, made a mess of a ballet step at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' turns DANCER into ANCER; with THE and T ('this at first') that is THEANCERT, 'botched' into the answer. Read whole, the clue describes a ballet leap a dancer might fluff.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballet jump in which the feet beat together in the air is exactly what a flustered dancer might bungle.

clue.text: A girl returning to claim gold in miniature scene

indicators.note: to claim means the reversed letters take in the next piece
returning means the letters run back the other way

parts.note: maid is an old word for a girl
or is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: A young woman comes back to collect a gold prize in a tiny tableau.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns A MAID into DIAMA, which takes in OR ('to claim').
explanation.definitionFit: A three-dimensional model display, such as a museum tableau in a box, is a small-scale scene.

clue.text: Dishes, emptied, to be filled with bone powder (dull-coloured) in small amounts

indicators.note: to be filled with means the remaining outer letters hold the following pieces
emptied means only the outside letters of dishes remain

parts.note: a rib is a bone
sand is a fine powdery grit
drab means dull and colourless

explanation.surface: Empty plates get a dusting of dreary bonemeal, a little at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'emptied' leaves DS, which is 'to be filled with' RIB + SAND + DRAB.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something arriving bit by bit, in scattered trickles.

clue.text: Roaming US city — what could be great about that?

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the city's abbreviation
what could be signals a possible rearrangement of the word great

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: Wandering through an American city, a visitor wonders what's so great about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what could be' rearranges GREAT, and that goes 'about' LA.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone free and roaming about, like an escaped prisoner, is described with this phrase.

clue.text: Knight ultimately the giddy limit — will stand and charge down imaginary foes

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of Knight
giddy means dizzy and spinning, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A knight finds it all too much and will make a stand, charging phantom enemies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives T from Knight; with LIMIT, WILL and STAND the letters are 'giddy'. The knight of the surface is Don Quixote, who attacked windmills thinking them giants.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from Don Quixote's mistaking windmills for giants, means attacking enemies that exist only in one's mind.

clue.text: Still tucking into other special snack

indicators.note: tucking into means the first piece goes inside the next

parts.note: else means other, as in 'someone else'
still can mean even, as in 'even/still better'

explanation.surface: Someone is still tucking into yet another special treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' reads as eating, but here it is a container indicator; 'Still' means even, as in 'still better'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain this is the light mid-morning bite with tea or coffee, around eleven o'clock.

clue.text: Team confronted with rugby player's facial hair

parts.note: a side is a team
a lock is a second-row forward in rugby; with 's it gives LOCKS

explanation.surface: A team squares up to a rugby forward with notable whiskers.
explanation.walkthrough: A lock is a position in rugby's scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Long locks of hair growing at the sides of the face, near the temples, count as hair framing the face.

clue.text: Risky losing leader without thinking things through

indicators.note: losing leader means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: hairy is informal for dangerous or risky

explanation.surface: A dangerous venture without a guide is rather careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing leader' takes the H from HAIRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Airy promises or an airy manner are breezy and casual, lacking serious consideration.

clue.text: Port worker's energy, describing American car?

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
a hand is a worker; the 's is a link
drive means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: A dock labourer's vigour is put to use describing a vehicle from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like a harbour but is the nautical word for left.
explanation.definitionFit: Cars in the US have the steering wheel on the left, so this phrase describes them; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Student got educated

parts.note: L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
earned means got, as in gained by work

explanation.surface: A pupil got an education.
explanation.walkthrough: L comes from the learner plates British drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholarly, well-read person is described as erudite or well schooled.

clue.text: Book African country shunning foremost holiday island

indicators.note: shunning foremost means the country loses its first letter

parts.note: Mali is in West Africa

explanation.surface: Reserve a trip to Africa while avoiding the most popular spots, opting for an island break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shunning foremost' drops M from MALI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indonesian island is a popular tourist destination, a classic beach getaway.

clue.text: Soldiers to abandon exhausted antelopes in coastal area

indicators.note: to abandon means the soldiers' letters leave the word for exhausted

parts.note: exhausted means tired
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
elands are large African antelopes

explanation.surface: Troops desert weary antelopes on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to abandon' takes RE (Royal Engineers) out of TIRED, leaving TID.
explanation.definitionFit: Land along the shore that is covered and uncovered by the sea's ebb and flow is a coastal zone.

clue.text: Framers of speech upset about representative's latest prepared comments

indicators.note: about means the mouth parts go round the next letter
upset in a down clue means the letters are turned upside down, read from the bottom

parts.note: the lips frame and shape spoken words

indicators.note: latest takes the final letter of representative's, ignoring the 's

explanation.surface: Speakers get flustered over a delegate's last rehearsed remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latest' gives E (last letter of 'representative'); LIPS goes 'about' it, making LEIPS, and 'upset' reads that upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A salesman's patter or rehearsed pitch is a set speech delivered from memory.

clue.text: Venue where there's an air of expectancy?

definitions.text: Venue where there's an air of expectancy?

parts.words: Venue where there's an air of expectancy?
parts.note: expectancy here means expecting a baby, so the venue is where pregnant women attend checkups

explanation.walkthrough: 'an air of expectancy' sounds like suspense, but 'expecting' also means pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Pregnant women, who are 'expecting', visit this medical centre before giving birth.

clue.text: Assistance bringing in river — will address such a state

definitions.note: the phrase points to a condition, read as 'in a dry condition', which the adjective describes

indicators.note: bringing in means the river letter is placed inside

parts.note: aid means help or assistance

explanation.surface: Relief that brings water from a river will tackle a drought-stricken land.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue links the two halves: aid (assistance) will address a parched condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Parched, waterless land is the condition that bringing water in would relieve.

clue.text: Finishes including it with latest of hit songs

indicators.note: including means the word for finishes holds the following letters

parts.note: dies means ends or finishes

indicators.note: latest of takes the final letter of hit

explanation.surface: A chart run ends, the latest hit included among the tunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finishes' is a verb here (dies = ends), not a noun, and 'including' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Short simple tunes or jingles are light pieces of music for singing.

clue.text: Meadows retreating around hot semi-arid region

indicators.note: around means the reversed letters surround the next piece
retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: leas are meadows or grassland
H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Grasslands receding around a hot, dry zone suggest desertification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreating' turns LEAS into SAEL, which goes 'around' H.
explanation.definitionFit: The belt of dry savannah south of the Sahara in Africa is a semi-desert zone.
